extracted.intended_audience: playwrights and poets writing heroic drama (Restoration/17th-century English stage)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating 'heroic plays' (verse dramas modeled on epic/heroic poetry), covering style, subject, plot, spectacle, supernatural elements, and character plausibility. Geared toward dramatists aiming to raise the stage above ordinary conversation and to imitate the grandeur of epic verse in a five-act drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heroic verse (avoid close imitation of conversation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Serious plays ought not to imitate conversation too nearly... very few tragedies, in this age, shall be received without it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden argues that serious/heroic plays should be written in exalted verse rather than prose because poetry allows thoughts to be raised above ordinary conversation; verse distinguishes poetry from mere imitation of daily speech and is necessary for the poetic effect. He acknowledges difficulty of verse but insists it often improves even imperfect writers by its sound and elevated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate an heroic poem (subject: love and valour)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An heroic play ought to be an imitation, in little, of an heroic poem; and, consequently, that love and valour ought to be the subject of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroic play should model itself on the laws and scope of epic/heroic poetry — treating grand passions and deeds (especially love and martial glory). Dryden cites Ariosto's programme (women, knights, arms, loves, courtesies, bold exploits) and uses such subjects to justify the elevated treatment and liberties of heroic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise thoughts and images above ordinary life (exalted style)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If nothing were to be raised above that level, the foundation of poetry would be destroyed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aim merely to mimic everyday speech or naturalistic detail; heroic drama permits and requires a heightened diction, imagery, and action to reach the 'perfection of art.' This elevation justifies departures from literal realism and from purely conversational language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include supernatural and visionary elements when poetically justified
rubrics_metrics.description: "An heroic poet is not tied to a bare representation of what is true, or exceeding probable; but that he may let himself loose to visionary objects..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden defends ghosts, gods, enchantments, and similar devices (Polydorus's ghost, enchanted wood, Bower of Bliss) as legitimate poetic tools. Objections that such elements are 'unnatural' are answered by noting their longstanding place in epic poetry and popular belief; supernatural material gives scope for imagination and poetic explanation of dark problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ spectacle (drums, trumpets, battles) to persuade the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "To those who object my frequent use of drums and trumpets, and my representations of battles, I answer... these warlike instruments, and even their presentations of fighting on the stage, are no more than necessary to produce the effects of an heroic play..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage effects, martial music, and battle-scenes — whether actually shown or heard — are tools to raise the audience's imagination and make them feel that what they behold is really performed. Dryden points to precedents (Shakespeare, Jonson) and argues these are essential for the intended dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide fullness of plot and a variety of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden criticises earlier experiments (D'Avenant's Siege of Rhodes) for lacking "the fulness of a plot, and the variety of characters to form it as it ought."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A heroic play must not be mere sketch or narration; it should supply a well-designed plot with multiple characters and situations to achieve the grandeur associated with epic imitation. Variety and structural design are required to elevate the piece beyond a fragmentary or one-dimensional spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer enacted action to mere narration
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is rather a play in narration, as I may call it, than an heroic poem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert the stage into a recited epic; the drama must present events visibly rather than rely on offstage report or long narrative passages. Showing action onstage is central to dramatic effect in heroic plays, even when borrowing epic scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to dominate spectators' imagination (create persuasive illusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poet is then to endeavour an absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators; for, though our fancy will..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The playwright's objective is to persuade and transport the audience — using language, spectacle, and elevated incident to create a temporary conviction that the heroic events are real. All artistic choices should serve that persuasive imaginative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate occasional disproportion or extravagance within the heroic mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott: "If the reader can abstract his mind from the qualities now deemed essential to a play, and consider the Conquest of Granada as a piece of romantic poetry, there are few compositions... which convey a more lively and favourable display... Amid the splendid ornaments of the structure we lose sight of occasional disproportion and incongruity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing within the romantic/heroic tradition, some excesses of scale, improbability, or rhetorical extravagance may be acceptable and even effective; they should be weighed against the poem's overall magnificence and imaginative power rather than judged solely by realistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain character consistency and believable motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott criticises Almanzor's "extravagant egotism" and Lyndaraxa's treachery as unjustified: motives and language must fit the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in elevated heroic drama, actions and speech should be grounded in character psychology; extravagant declarations can be explained by passion but should not undermine a character's credibility onstage. Motivations (e.g., treachery, self-sacrifice) need plausible grounding to be accepted by audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance heroic individual feats with historical or genre plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott: single-man feats were sometimes plausible in earlier ages or romance, but the "gross improbability of a hero, by his single arm, turning the tide of battle..." can be objectionable unless historically or conventionally justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary feats of a single hero are acceptable within the conventions of chivalric romances or historical contexts that historically valorized individual prowess; otherwise the playwright should provide context or conventions that make such feats believable to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft subplots (especially love-episodes) with beauty and ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott: "the under plot of the loves of Ozmyn and Benzayda is beautiful in itself, and ingeniously managed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use secondary plots to complement the central heroic action. Well-managed love-subplots can humanize heroic figures, offer contrast, and increase the play's emotional and structural richness; they should be well-integrated and artfully handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal locality and cultural specificity for foreign/ethnic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott notes a defect: "although the characters are called Moors, there is scarce any expression, or allusion, which can fix the reader's attention upon their locality..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting a play among a particular people or place (e.g., Moors of Granada), include linguistic touches, references, or cultural particulars to root characters in their setting and make the scene convincing; generic heroics alone may flatten cultural identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the appropriate thematic stakes (e.g., patriotism for national crises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott criticises that during the siege of Granada "the principle of patriotism is hardly once alluded to... the fate, or the wishes, of Almahide, Lyndaraxa, and Benzayda, are all that interest the Moorish warriors... as if the Christian was not thundering at their gates."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dramatic situation involves broader social, political, or national stakes (siege, war, national peril), these larger themes should be acknowledged and integrated, rather than focusing solely on private passions; this grounds the heroic action in consequential stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let passion justify heightened rhetoric, but ensure theatrical suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott and Dryden discuss that passion may produce 'talking nonsense' yet question whether such ranting is suitable to display heroic character on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heightened rhetoric and extravagant addresses can convey heroic intensity, but the playwright must judge whether such speech serves theatrical effectiveness. Passion may excuse excess, but onstage language should still reveal character and be performable/convincing to spectators.
